title: Two Very Different Pop-Up Debates on the Same Day
author: Stuart Jr., Dave
summary: Dave Stuart Jr. compares the first pop-up debate of the year in two of his world history classes held on the same day, one of the best he has seen in years and the other a typical humdrum first attempt. He recounts the simple rules, the strengths and weaknesses the first class identified, and the low volunteerism and repetitive agreement of the second. Acknowledging that classrooms contain countless variables, he settles on the strongest explanation he can see: in the first hour a few students put themselves out there, and that boldness proved contagious. His response is practical. He will identify a few students in the quieter class and encourage them through a moment of genuine connection to lead off next time. He will also push the stronger class quickly into a harder topic to show he means it when he says they do hard things.
points: Two classes under identical conditions can perform very differently, and a few early risk-takers can set the tone for an entire discussion.
Framing debate as a team sport in which students are mental athletes makes the whole-class performance the unit of improvement.
Having students name one strength and one weakness of the group debrief builds shared standards for discussion.
Moments of genuine connection serve double duty, strengthening motivation beliefs and lifting the academic performance of the whole class.
quotes: So after the debate was through, I had students identify one strength and one weakness in our whole-class performance. I used this mini-prompt as a chance to explain what I’ll repeat often this year: pop-up debate is a team sport, and in this sport we are all mental athletes. Debates will flourish or flounder based not on individuals, but on the team.

So my goal between this week and next is to identify a few students in that second class who I think could go there and to encourage them in a moment of genuine connection to do it in our next debate.

Moments of genuine connection, in this case, are a tool not just for improving the five key beliefs in my students — they are also elegantly efficient levers for increasing the academic (in this case, argumentative) performance of the entire class.

And of course, in that first class, the key right now is to quickly follow up with another debate, perhaps this time on a more challenging, less immediately “relevant” topic, so as to show them that I mean it when I say that we do hard things.
